alt: Left: height varies continuously and is plotted as a histogram with touching bars and a bell-shaped curve. Right: ABO blood group varies discontinuously into A, B, AB and O, plotted as a bar chart with separate bars. Below, genetic causes are mutation, meiosis and random fertilisation; environmental causes are diet, light, temperature and soil minerals.
caption: Continuous variation needs a histogram; discontinuous variation needs a bar chart.

alt: Five steps with beetles on bark. 1: pale and dark beetles vary and colour is inherited. 2: ash darkens the bark and birds hunt by sight. 3: pale beetles are seen and eaten more. 4: surviving dark beetles breed and pass on the dark allele. 5: over many generations most beetles are dark.
caption: Variation, selection pressure, survival, inheritance, many generations: give every link.

alt: Four panels. Fossils in rock layers, with deeper layers usually older. Homologous five-digit limbs in a human arm, a bat wing and a whale flipper suggest a common ancestor. Illustrative DNA sequences: species Y differs from X at one base and Z at four, so X and Y share a more recent ancestor. Antibiotic and pesticide resistance can be observed within a lifetime.
caption: Fossils, anatomy, molecules and observed change all point to common ancestry.

alt: An energy pyramid for a fictional grassland: producers 24 000, primary consumers 2160 and secondary consumers 216 kJ per square metre per year, transfers of 9.0% and 10%. The rest is lost as heat from respiration, in movement and in parts not eaten or digested. Below, energy pyramids are always pyramid-shaped, pyramids of numbers can be inverted, as with one oak and many caterpillars, and biomass pyramids are usually upright.
caption: Only about a tenth of the energy passes up each level, so chains stay short.

alt: A graph of population size against time. Prey numbers rise and fall in a cycle; predator numbers follow the same cycle but peak later, after a lag. Prey rise, predators rise with more food, prey fall as more are eaten, predators fall with less food, and prey recover.
caption: The predator peak always comes after the prey peak.

alt: Three rows of plus, zero and minus signs. Mutualism (plus, plus): Rhizobium in legume root nodules fixes nitrogen and the plant supplies sugars. Commensalism (plus, zero): barnacles on a whale gain transport and feeding. Parasitism (plus, minus): a tapeworm absorbs digested food in its host’s gut.
caption: Symbiosis types differ in who gains and who loses.

alt: Top: ten random 0.5 m quadrats in a 40 m by 25 m field count 3, 0, 5, 2, 4, 1, 6, 2, 3 and 4 daisies; mean 3.0, density 12 per square metre, estimate 12 000. Bottom: 48 woodlice are marked and released; a second sample of 60 contains 12 marked, so N = 48 × 60 ÷ 12 = 240, assuming marks stay on, animals mix, and no births, deaths or migration.
caption: Scale up from a sample: quadrats for plants, capture–mark–recapture for animals that move.
